transcript.text: panasonic nn h98 not heating anymore, any fix?

If your Panasonic NN‑H98 powers on and the turntable/light/fan run but it no longer heats food, the fault is usually in the high-voltage/inverter system rather than a simple setting.

Try these safe checks first:

1. Power reset
• Unplug it for 5–10 minutes.
• Plug it directly into a known-good wall outlet (not an extension lead).
• Set the clock if required and test with a mug of water for 60 seconds on full power.

2. Check settings
• Ensure it is on Microwave / High / 100% power, not a defrost, low-power, timer, or demo mode.
• Make sure the door closes firmly and nothing is obstructing the latch.

3. Observe what happens
• Runs normally but food stays cold: commonly magnetron, inverter board, high-voltage diode/capacitor, or a thermal cut-out.
• Stops after a few seconds, flashes an error, or makes unusual buzzing/arcing noises: stop using it and have it inspected.
• Dead/no display: could be mains fuse, door switch, thermal fuse, or control board.

Do not remove the cover or try to test internal components yourself. Microwaves contain a high-voltage capacitor that can retain a dangerous charge even after unplugging.

For a Panasonic inverter microwave, a “runs but doesn’t heat” fault is often an inverter PCB or magnetron issue. These can be repairable, but the cost may approach replacement cost depending on the unit’s age. A microwave repair technician can diagnose it quickly.

If you provide the full model number from the rating label (usually inside the door frame or on the back), plus whether it runs normally or shows any error/noise, I can narrow down the likely fault.
sorry h98 is what the screen says when it stops, the model on the back is nn-cd87ksbpq. microwave mode runs a few seconds then stops with h98, grill still works

On the Panasonic NN-CD87KSBPQ, H98 is a fault in the microwave high-voltage/inverter system. In practice, it usually means the inverter power supply, magnetron, associated wiring, or an overheat/protection component has failed or is being detected as faulty.

The fact that:

• microwave mode starts, then stops after a few seconds with H98
• grill still works

strongly supports that diagnosis. The grill circuit is separate, so it can work normally even when the microwave-generation system has shut down.

### What you can safely try
1. Unplug it for 10–15 minutes, then retry with a cup of water on full microwave power.
2. Make sure the air vents are clear, the oven is not tightly enclosed, and the cavity is empty except for the water test.
3. If it has recently been very hot or used for long periods, let it cool completely and retry once.

If H98 returns, it is not a user-resettable error and continued microwave use is not recommended.

### What not to do
Do not remove the outer case or attempt to test/replace the inverter, magnetron, capacitor, or related parts. Microwaves contain potentially lethal high voltage even after being unplugged.

### Repair options
It needs a Panasonic-authorised or microwave-qualified repairer. Likely repair possibilities include:

• inverter board replacement/repair
• magnetron replacement
• thermal protector or connection fault

The inverter/magnetron repair can be expensive, so ask for a diagnosis/quote before authorising work. You can generally still use grill-only functions if they operate normally, but avoid any microwave or combination programme, as those use the faulty microwave system.
tried unplugging it, same h98 again. cup of water stops after about 10-15 seconds and the water's still cold. is it worth repairing?

With that behaviour, it is almost certainly an H98 inverter/high-voltage microwave fault, not a resettable issue. It detects the fault after roughly 10–15 seconds and deliberately stops microwave operation. The cold water confirms it is not producing microwave energy.

### Is repair worth it?
Usually, it depends mainly on the oven’s age and the repair quote:

• Less than about 3–4 years old: generally worth getting a diagnosis and quote. This is a premium combination microwave and replacement is relatively costly.
• Around 5 years or older: it can be borderline. Inverter or magnetron repairs can make economic sense only if the total is modest.
• If the repair quote is more than roughly 40–50% of a comparable replacement: replacement is usually the sensible option.

Typical UK ballpark figures, though they vary by area and parts availability:

• Diagnosis/call-out: £60–£120
• Inverter board repair/replacement: often £150–£300+ total
• Magnetron replacement: often £180–£350+ total

H98 more commonly points toward the inverter PCB/system, but a technician needs to confirm whether the inverter, magnetron, wiring, or a protection device is responsible.

### Before paying out
1. Check your purchase date, receipt, retailer cover, credit-card cover, or any Panasonic extended warranty.
2. If it is relatively new, contact the retailer/Panasonic first. In the UK, the Consumer Rights Act can sometimes help with an appliance that has not lasted a reasonable time, even after the initial guarantee—though evidence of an inherent fault may be needed after the first six months.
3. Obtain a fixed diagnostic charge and a “do not repair above £X without approval” instruction.

### In the meantime
Do not use microwave or combination modes. Grill-only use is electrically separate and is likely safe if it operates normally, but if you notice burning smells, unusual noise, sparking, or any other errors, stop using the appliance entirely.

If you tell me roughly when you bought it and what a similar replacement costs where you are, I can give a clearer repair-versus-replace recommendation.
its about 6 years old, cost around £300. would pay for a sensible repair but not sure what's sensible

For a ~6-year-old NN-CD87KSBPQ that cost about £300, I’d set a fairly firm repair limit:

• Up to £100–£120 total: sensible to repair.
• £120–£150 total: reasonable if you otherwise like the oven and it is in good condition.
• £150–£180: borderline; only worth it if the repairer gives a solid warranty on the repair/part.
• Over ~£180: I would usually replace it rather than repair it.
• £220+: almost certainly replace.

That is because H98 is often an inverter board or magnetron issue, and either can be a substantial repair. On a six-year-old combination microwave, there is also a chance another age-related component fails later.

When contacting a repairer, say:

> Panasonic NN-CD87KSBPQ combination microwave. Microwave starts but stops after 10–15 seconds with H98; grill works. Please quote diagnostic cost and do not proceed if total repair exceeds £150 without contacting me.

Ask specifically:
• Is the diagnostic fee deducted from the repair price?
• Is the quote inclusive of labour, VAT, call-out and parts?
• Is it the inverter PCB, magnetron, or something else?
• What warranty applies to the repair? Ideally 6–12 months.

If it turns out to be a simple connection, thermal cut-out, or repairable inverter-board fault, it may land in the worthwhile range. If it needs a new inverter assembly or magnetron and the quote is near £200+, replacement is the better bet.
